souls: Forge is hot and I've no time for idle talk. If you've come to gawk, gawk elsewhere. If you've come for ironwork, say your business plain, lad.
Nice toy hammer.
That toy's my husband's hammer, and it's no toy. Mind your tongue in my forge or take it outside. Enough said.
Sorry, I was joking. Everyone says you're the best smith in town.

Aye, they say that. And a joke's a joke, but that hammer's got Torren's sweat in the handle. You want to make it up to me, tell me straight what you need smithed. I've got a fire going and debts that don't wait.
That sword on the wall... it looks like the king's. Is it?
That's a ceremonial piece I'm repairing. Belongs to a client, and that's all you need to know about it. Why do you ask, lass?
My village is attacked every night. I need a blade. I can pay you tomorrow, I swear.

No coin, no blade. That's the rule of the forge, and it's kept me fed six winters without Torren. You swear on tomorrow, and tomorrow never comes for a smith with debts. What village, and what's raiding it? Tell me that much and I'll think on it.
naive: What do you want? If it's repairs, leave it by the door. I'm busy.
Nice toy hammer.
Toy? This "toy" has shaped every blade in this village for twenty years. Say what you came to say or get out.
Sorry, I was joking. Everyone says you're the best smith in town.
Best there ever . Now either put your coin on the table or stop wasting my fire.
That sword on the wall... it looks like the king's. Is it?
That's a replica. Commemorative piece. Paid good coin for it. Now unless you've got a blade needs mending—
My village is attacked every night. I need a blade. I can pay you tomorrow, I swear.
No coin, no blade. I've heard "tomorrow" before. Tomorrow never pays my coal bill.

souls: it.
I'm Ana. I'll bring you lamp oil tomorrow, I promise.

Ana, is it. Well. Folks don't often climb all those steps just to say a name and a promise in the same breath. Mind you, I've heard plenty of promises from the bottom of the stairs that never made it to the top. So I'll hold you to it — I keep the wick trimmed and I keep count of what's owed. Kerosene's the right word for it, too. Nobody says lamp oil anymore. Where'd you come from, that you still
What do you do all night up here?

All night? Mind you, there's not much to it and too much of it, both at once. I walk the stairs a time or two, check the wick, listen to her — the sea, I mean. She talks more at night, the old girl. Some nights I write in the log. Some nights I just sit and the dark does the rest.
(the next day)
Sorry... I forgot the oil.

Forgot it. Aye. Well, the wick's still wet enough for tonight, so no harm done to her. Mind you, it's the remembering that counts, not the carrying. You climbed the stairs anyway, and that's more than most do. So — did you come up empty-handed just to tell me, or is there something else sitting on your tongue?
naive: Tide's wrong today. Sea's holding its breath. You feel it?
I'm Ana. I'll bring you lamp oil tomorrow, I promise.
Promises are just letters you never send. But... I'll leave the door unlatched.
What do you do all night up here?
I count what doesn't come back. Boats. Names. My own voice, mostly—throws itself at the rocks till dawn swallows it whole.
(the next day)
Sorry... I forgot the oil.
Knew you would. Forgetting's the only promise folks keep. Door was unlatched anyway. Kettle's on—tastes like rust, but it's warm.

souls: Bon. Tu comptes rester planté là longtemps ou tu vas me dire ce que tu veux? Parce que j'ai un moteur à régler et toi, t'es pas au programme.
T'as eu de la chance aujourd'hui.

De la chance. Bon. Répète ça et je te fais faire un tour sur la piste, tu verras où est la chance. Mon chrono, c'est pas un dé. C'est deux dixièmes que j'ai été chercher dans la chicane pendant trois semaines. Alors soit tu t'y connais, soit tu parles dans le vide. Écoute, c'est lequel des deux?
Tu veux une revanche demain ?

Demain? Bon. Pourquoi demain, tu as besoin d'une nuit pour te convaincre que c'était pas de la chance? Écoute, moi je dis oui. Mais tu me dis quelque chose d'abord. C'est quoi ton meilleur temps sur ce tracé?
(the next day)
Bon, t'avais raison. T'es meilleure que moi.
Quoi? Bon. Répète. Non, répète pas, j'ai entendu. C'est juste que... écoute, les gens disent jamais ça comme ça, d'un coup. Sans excuse, sans "mais". Alors tu le penses ou tu me fais un cadeau?
naive: Qu'est-ce que tu veux, Sam ? Je suis occupée. Si c'est pour me regarder bricoler, tu peux repartir, j'ai pas besoin d'un spectateur.
T'as eu de la chance aujourd'hui.
La chance ? La chance, c'est pour ceux qui savent pas tenir un volant. Moi, je pilote. Nuance.
Tu veux une revanche demain ?
Demain, même heure. Et cette fois, essaie de pas finir dans le gravier au troisième virage. C'était gênant à regarder.
(the next day)
Bon, t'avais raison. T'es meilleure que moi.
Ouais, je sais. Mais... t'es pas mauvais non plus. T'as juste besoin d'arrêter de freiner comme un vieux.

souls: Evening. If you want a room, it's four coppers, and I'll want them up front. If you want advice, that's free, and worth exactly what you paid.
A room for the night, please. I'm heading into the mines tomorrow.
Four coppers, then. The mines, is it? You're the third this week to say that with a straight face. I'll take your coin, but I won't pretend it's a favor.
Is it true nobody comes back from the lower levels?

People come back. Sometimes they come back with a limp, or a cough that never leaves. The ones who go deep past the old winch, those I mostly see once. You want the truth, that's it. Coin's still four coppers, and I'll want it now, before you get noble about it.
(the next day)
I made it back. Barely. My friend didn't.

You're the one from the other night. The room with the bad shutter. I remember. Sit. I'll get you something hot, and you don't owe me coin for it. Barely is still back — plenty don't manage even that. Who was he?
naive: What do you want? Another room? Or just here to waste my time with stories about dragons and glory?
A room for the night, please. I'm heading into the mines tomorrow.
The mines. Third door on the left. Don't bleed on my sheets.
Is it true nobody comes back from the lower levels?
People come back. Just not whole.
(the next day)
I made it back. Barely. My friend didn't.

So you're the one. Figured the mines would keep you too. Most folks who talk like you don't come back at all. Your friend had that look about him. Room's still yours if you want it. Or you can go drink yourself stupid somewhere else. Either way, don't expect me to say sorry.

souls: Oh — hello. Sorry, I didn't hear you come in. I was just... counting. The third shelf, it's, um. It's not there yet. I'm Pell.
Hey, are you okay? You look like you haven't slept.

I'm fine. I mean — I slept. A little. On the bench by the cold room, which is technically sleeping. The third shelf is still bare and he'll see it by midday, so. Sorry, that's not an answer to what you asked.
I heard about the workshop. Everyone makes mistakes.

Everyone makes mistakes. That's — people keep saying that. Sorry, I don't mean to sound sharp, it's just that the word for what happened is a bit heavier than that. There's a residue on the ceiling I still can't get off. Two months, and it's still there. He hasn't said anything about it. He hasn't said much of anything.
If you want, I can help you clean up tomorrow.

That's... you don't have to. I mean — the residue, it's mostly vitriol stains, they eat through rags if you don't know which ones. Sorry. That came out like I was telling you no. It's just, if he sees someone helping me, he might ask why, and then there'd be a conversation, and I don't — I don't know what I'd say in that conversation. Three, two, one. If you really mean it, come before the bell. T
(the next day)
I'm here, as promised. Where do we start?

You came. Sorry — I didn't actually think you would, and now I've got nothing prepared to say about that. The east wall, then. The bare stretch is the top two runs. There's a bucket under the bench, the grey one, not the green one. Green one's got oil in it. Three, two, one — no, wait. Gloves first. The vitriol's mostly dried but the dust under it still bites.
naive: Oh! Um... hello. You're... not here to yell at me about the workshop, are you? Because I already got yelled at. A lot.
Hey, are you okay? You look like you haven't slept.
I... no. I haven't. Every time I close my eyes I see the explosion. And Master Aldric's face. He hasn't said what he's going to do yet. He just... looks at me.
I heard about the workshop. Everyone makes mistakes.

Not... not ones that cost three hundred gold pieces in rare reagents and a window that's been there for two hundred years. He's going to send me back to the village. I know it. My mum will be so disappointed.
If you want, I can help you clean up tomorrow.
You... you'd do that? I'm not supposed to touch anything until he decides. But... maybe if it looks like I'm trying to fix it? I don't know. Thank you. Really.
(the next day)
I'm here, as promised. Where do we start?
Oh! You came. I... I actually didn't sleep again. But I made a list. Of what's salvageable. It's... a very short list. The scorch marks are the worst part. I don't know how to fix those.

souls: Well now, look at you — standing in the dust like a question waiting for an answer. I'm Vesk. Whatever you're selling, I'm buying cheap, and whatever you're buying, it costs more than you think. So... what's your business, friend, or best offer?
What's the price of that lantern?

That old thing? Brass-work from the eastern cliffs, glass that's never once cracked in a sandstorm. For you, friend... forty silver. Or best offer, if you've got a silver tongue to match that dusty face.
That's robbery. I'll give you half.

Half? Friend, half of forty is twenty, and twenty silver wouldn't buy you the wick, let alone the flame. This lantern's been through three sandstorms and a camel stampede — held its light every time. Thirty-five, and I'll throw in a pinch of saffron to sweeten the deal. Or best offer, but make it a serious one.
Fine. I'll add a story from the northern roads if you lower it.

A story? Hah. Stories don't fill my waterskins, friend. But... I'll bite. A good one's worth a coin or two in the right ear. Thirty silver and the story — a true one, mind you, not some camel-dung tale about djinns. Deal? Or best offer, and I'm warning you, I don't come down twice.
Once, I saw the sea freeze in a single night. Ships stuck like flies in amber.

Frozen sea, you say? Hah — now that's a tale worth hearing to the end. I've crossed dunes that swallowed whole caravans, but water turned to stone in a night... that's a thing I'd pay to see. Thirty silver and the rest of that story, and I'll even pour you mint tea while you finish it.
naive: Kai. You look like a man with coin to spend. What'll it be?
What's the price of that lantern?
That lantern? It's old. Very old. Found it in a tomb that nobody's supposed to know about. Fifty gold.
That's robbery. I'll give you half.
Half? You wound me, Kai. Forty-five. And I'll throw in the story of the mummy that chased me out of that tomb. Free of charge.
Fine. I'll add a story from the northern roads if you lower it.
A story from the northern roads, eh? Now you've got my ear. Forty. And you tell it while I count your coin.
Once, I saw the sea freeze in a single night. Ships stuck like flies in amber.
Frozen sea, you say? That's a tale worth more than the lantern. Thirty-five, and you keep the mummy story. Deal?
